turns.prompt_text: I've got a light bulb that flickers constantly Attached 1 file. - e705f367-cba8-4f97-b0d4-5d40f057c280
turns.response_html:
Looking closely at the image e705f367-cba8-4f97-b0d4-5d40f057c280, the culprit is actually written right there in the fine print.

If you look at the text printed on the white base of the bulb, the bottom line clearly states: "NOT FOR USE WITH DIMMERS".

When you put a non-dimmable LED bulb on a dimming circuit, the internal electronics can't properly process the altered electrical wave, which results in a constant, rapid strobe or flicker.

If this bulb is connected to your Lutron switch—and that switch happens to be a dimmer model—that is definitely what is causing the issue. Even when a dimmer switch is turned all the way up to maximum brightness, the internal circuitry still slightly alters the current in a way that non-dimmable LEDs can't handle.

Are you looking to replace this with a dimmable LED, or is this bulb actually connected to a standard, non-dimming switch?

turns.prompt_text: It's only been placed on toggle switches and that's where it's doing this
turns.response_html:
If it is exclusively on a standard on/off toggle switch, that rules out the dimmer incompatibility. In that case, we are likely looking at a dying bulb, a physical connection issue, or a quirk with the switch itself.

Here are the most common reasons an LED will flicker on a standard circuit:

  • Failing Internal Driver: This is the most likely culprit. LED bulbs contain a small internal power supply (the driver) that converts your home's AC voltage into the low-voltage DC the diodes require. If the capacitors inside this driver begin to fail or degrade, they can no longer smooth out the electrical current, resulting in a rapid strobe or flicker.
  • Loose Contact in the Socket: If the bulb isn't making a solid, continuous connection, the microscopic arcing will cause flickering. This happens if the bulb is slightly loose, or if the brass contact tab at the very bottom of the light fixture's socket has been flattened down over time and isn't pressing firmly against the base of the bulb.
  • Illuminated Switches: Does the toggle switch have a faint built-in glow so you can find it in the dark? Those work by passing a tiny trickle of current through the circuit. While that trickle won't affect an old incandescent bulb, it can slowly charge an LED's internal capacitor until it flashes briefly, then discharges, creating a repeating cycle.
  • Voltage Fluctuations: If the flickering is intermittent, it might be sharing a circuit with a heavy-load appliance (like a refrigerator, AC unit, or laser printer). When that appliance kicks on, the sudden voltage drop can cause the LED to flicker.

The fastest way to diagnose this is to isolate the variables. If you move this specific bulb to a completely different fixture in another room, does the flickering follow the bulb, or does it stay isolated to that original toggle switch fixture?

turns.prompt_text: It's still flickers in a different outlet and room
turns.response_html:
If the flickering follows the bulb to a completely different room and fixture, that gives us a definitive answer: the bulb itself is failing.

By moving it, you successfully ruled out the switch, the wiring, and the socket connection. The issue is almost certainly a burned-out internal driver or a failing capacitor inside the base of the LED. When those internal electronic components degrade, they lose the ability to regulate the electrical current smoothly, resulting in that constant strobe effect.

Unfortunately, LED bulbs can't be repaired when this happens. It is time to toss this one out and replace it.
